summaries.example: Imagine a soccer team. At first, you may copy one teammate's move. Later, you learn what every player is supposed to do. You can then think about your own place in the whole game. Mead says this helps a self grow. Your quick, new move is like the “I.” Your understanding of your team role is like the “Me.”
summaries.summary:
George Herbert Mead was an American philosopher and social theorist connected with pragmatism, a tradition that studies ideas through their effects in real life. He explained that a person does not develop a mind and a self all alone. Communication, especially language, lets us hear our own words and imagine how others will respond. This ability helps us think about ourselves.

Mead also explained self-development through roles. A child pretending to be a doctor must imagine what a patient might say. In a game, a player must understand many positions and rules, not just one partner's actions. By learning the organized activity of a group, a person can look at their own behavior from the group's point of view. Mead called this shared viewpoint the generalized other.

He described two connected sides of action. The “Me” is the part of the self shaped by learned roles and group expectations. The “I” is the fresh response that happens in the moment. The “I” can be creative, and its new actions may change the group. Mead also believed that nature and history contain real change and emergence: new forms or possibilities can arise, so the future is not simply a repeat of the past.
key_ideas: People develop their minds and selves through communication with others.
Words become meaningful when speakers and listeners can understand and expect similar responses.
Playing roles helps us see situations from other people's points of view.
The “Me” includes learned expectations, while the “I” brings new action and creativity.
Mead thought change is real and that new possibilities can appear in nature and society.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mead's ideas help explain why friendships, families, teams, schools, and communities influence how people think about themselves. They also show that being shaped by others does not mean being completely fixed. People can respond in new ways and sometimes help change the groups they belong to. His work connects questions about identity, language, cooperation, learning, and freedom.

important_terms.definition: The way people understand themselves through communication and relationships with other people.
A word, sound, or action that means something shared by people who use it.
Thinking about how another person or group might respond, then using that understanding to guide your own action.
The organized group whose rules and expectations help a person understand their place in the group.
The fresh, partly unpredictable response a person makes in a situation.

questions_to_think_about: How do other people help you learn who you are?
When have you guessed what someone else was about to say or do?
Can a group change because one person tries something new?
Which parts of your behavior feel learned, and which feel spontaneous?

summaries.example: Consider a student joining a debate team. The student first learns specific exchanges with a partner: when one speaker makes a claim, the other answers with evidence. With practice, the student learns the positions and expectations of the entire debate format. This organized system becomes a generalized other, allowing the student to assess their own performance as a debater—the “Me.” Yet no rule mechanically determines the exact reply to a new argument. The student's inventive response expresses the “I,” and a successful new strategy may alter how the team approaches later debates.
summaries.summary:
George Herbert Mead develops a social theory of mind and self within American pragmatism. His central claim is not merely that society influences an already complete individual. Rather, language and interaction help constitute the capacities we recognize as mind and self. A gesture has meaning through the response it produces in another organism, but it becomes a significant symbol when speaker and hearer can anticipate functionally similar responses. Vocal language is especially important because the speaker can hear their own expression and thereby bring the social process into their own experience.

This reflexivity supports role-taking. People learn to respond from the standpoint of others, first in relatively simple interactions and then within organized activities. A game illustrates the difference: participants must understand the responses associated with many positions and the rules connecting them. Internalizing the perspective of the organized group creates the generalized other. The self is therefore social, cognitive, and related to self-consciousness rather than identical with the merely biological individual.

Mead distinguishes the “Me” and the “I” as functional phases, not separate metaphysical entities. The “Me” is the self as an object of reflection, formed through internalized roles and expectations. The “I” is the initiating response occurring in action. Its exact character is available only retrospectively, when it has become part of what can be known as a “Me.” Because the “I” can be novel, it may alter the habits and organization of a group, producing a changed self and a changed social system.

key_ideas: Mind is not adequately explained as an isolated property of an individual organism; it develops through social communication and reflexive activity.
A vocal gesture can become significant when the speaker can respond to it in a way that anticipates the hearer's response.
The self is socially constituted through role-taking and through internalizing the organized perspective of a generalized other.
The “Me” represents learned and organized social expectations, whereas the “I” introduces action that is novel and not fully predictable beforehand.
Mead's account of emergence challenges a picture of nature as completely predictable from prior conditions; novelty can transform both present arrangements and how the past is understood.

This account complicates the opposition between determinism and freedom: social conditions shape agents, but reflective, creative action can contribute to self-transformation and social reconstruction.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mead provides a way to connect personal identity with language, institutions, education, science, and democratic life without reducing persons either to isolated minds or to passive products of society. His distinction between the “I” and the “Me” explains how social learning and originality can coexist. His account of emergence also gives philosophical importance to genuine change: people may confront problems for which existing habits are inadequate, reflect on alternatives, and participate in reconstructing their selves and communities.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical tradition that evaluates ideas partly by how they function in experience, inquiry, and problem-solving.
A process in which a new feature or form arises from an earlier system and changes the relations within that system.
The capacity of experience or action to turn back upon itself, allowing a person to anticipate and assess responses, including their own.
A shared symbol, especially a vocal expression, that evokes sufficiently similar responses in speaker and hearer.
The organized community or system of roles whose viewpoint an individual internalizes.
The socially formed, reflectively knowable aspect of self related to learned expectations and organized activities.
The name Mead gives to the initiating, novel response that cannot be known in its exact form until after it occurs.
The transitional condition between an established order and a possible new order, while their relations are being adjusted.

questions_to_think_about: Does learning social expectations limit freedom, or can it provide the abilities needed for intelligent action?
Can a person have several “Me”s connected with different groups without lacking a unified self?
Why might Mead reject the idea that the “I” is a permanent hidden substance or soul?
How does the possibility of emergence affect arguments for or against determinism?
What would it mean to solve a moral problem by changing a social situation rather than merely choosing between existing options?

summaries.example: Suppose you join a new basketball team. At first, you learn what your coach and teammates expect from you. You may practice taking the role of a particular player, such as a guard. Soon, though, you must understand the whole game: where everyone moves, which rules apply, and what teammates may need next. The team becomes a “generalized other,” because you use the group's organized expectations to judge your own actions. If you invent a new pass during a difficult play, that fresh response is like Mead's “I.” If the team adopts it, the group—and your place in it—may change.
summaries.summary:
George Herbert Mead argues that the mind and self grow through social life. He was a pragmatist, meaning that he examined ideas in connection with experience, action, and problem-solving. For Mead, a gesture gets its meaning from how another organism responds. Animal signals can guide behavior, but human language can do more: a speaker can hear their own words and anticipate how another person will react. This shared, anticipated response makes a gesture a significant symbol.

Language allows people to become reflexive, or able to turn their experience back on themselves. We can think about what we are saying, predict how others may answer, and adjust our actions. This does not mean all thought is a private activity. Mead says that mind has a social basis because the responses of others become part of the resources we use in thinking.

The self develops further through role-taking. Pretending to be a doctor requires imagining a patient's responses. Participating in a game requires understanding the positions and rules of the whole activity. Mead calls the organized viewpoint of such a group the generalized other. It allows a person to judge their own behavior in relation to the group, not merely in relation to one individual.

Mead distinguishes the “Me” from the “I.” The “Me” is the organized, learned side of the self: the expectations and roles that we can reflect on. The “I” is the response that occurs in action. It is partly unpredictable and may be creative. We know it directly only after it has happened, when we can think about it as part of a “Me.” New responses may be taken up by a group and change its habits.

key_ideas: Mead connects the growth of language, mind, and self with social interaction rather than treating them as purely private abilities.
A person can use language to anticipate another person's response and also to respond internally to their own words.
Role-taking begins in simple interactions and becomes more complex when people learn the organized rules of groups and activities.
The “Me” reflects social expectations; the “I” supplies a response that is not completely determined in advance.
New actions can change a group, which can then change the selves of its members.
Mead's view of real change leaves room for freedom, although he did not give a complete theory of moral autonomy.
summaries.why_it_matters: Mead's theory helps explain how identity is shaped by conversations, teams, families, schools, and larger communities. It also avoids two extremes: the idea that people create themselves entirely alone, and the idea that social training determines every action. Because people can understand group expectations and respond creatively, they may help transform both themselves and the communities around them.

important_terms.definition: The idea that people understand themselves and their surroundings through practical activity and the results of ideas.
A sign or gesture that has a shared meaning because the sender and receiver can respond to it in similar ways.
Trying to understand another person's position, expectations, or likely response.
The viewpoint of an organized group, including its rules and the responses expected from its members.
The learned, organized side of the self that reflects group expectations and can be considered as an object.
The spontaneous and sometimes creative response made in a particular situation.
The appearance of something genuinely new that can change an existing system.
The in-between period when an old pattern is changing and a new pattern has not yet settled.

questions_to_think_about: How is taking a role in a game different from simply copying another person?
Why does Mead think the self is not the same thing as the biological individual?
Can the expectations of a group both guide and restrict your choices?
What might happen when a new action does not fit an old group pattern?
How could reflecting on a difficult situation help someone become a different kind of person?
